title: Impact of Paid Family Leave on Women's Labor Force Participation

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Two–way-fixed-effects Difference-in-Differences (DID)

• Rationale – We observe states that adopt a paid-family-leave (PFL) law (treated = 1) and states that never adopt (treated = 0), both before (post = 0) and after (post = 1) adoption. The interaction treat_x_post is the policy “shock.”  
• Key identifying assumptions  
 1. Parallel trends – In the absence of PFL, the log labor-force-participation trajectories of treated and control states would have evolved in parallel.  
 2. No simultaneous confounders – No other state-level reform coincides perfectly with PFL adoption and differentially affects women’s labor supply.  
 3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA) – A state’s PFL law does not spill over to women in other states.  

We implement a two-way FE regression (state and period) with cluster-robust SE at the state level, plus robustness checks: (i) a plain DID without fixed effects, (ii) a placebo test using only pre-treatment periods, and (iii) adding state-specific linear trends.



## 2. R Code
```r
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Impact of Paid Family Leave on Women's Labor-Force Participation
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Required packages
pkgs <- c("data.table", "fixest")
to_install <- pkgs[!pkgs %in% installed.packages()[, "Package"]]
if(length(to_install)) install.packages(to_install, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
library(data.table)   # fast import / manipulation
library(fixest)       # fast FE estimators w/ easy clustering

# 1. Read the data -----------------------------------------------------------
dat_path <- "experiments/exp_b/data/s42_data.csv"
dt <- fread(dat_path)

# 2. Main DID with two-way fixed effects -------------------------------------
did_twfe <- feols(y ~ treat_x_post | unit_id + period, 
                  data = dt, cluster = ~unit_id)

# 3. Baseline DID without FE (textbook spec) ---------------------------------
did_plain <- feols(y ~ treated + post + treat_x_post, 
                   data = dt, cluster = ~unit_id)

# 4. Placebo test – only pre-treatment periods -------------------------------
dt_pre  <- dt[post == 0]               # keep observations before adoption
placebo <- feols(y ~ treated, 
                 data = dt_pre, cluster = ~unit_id)

# 5. Robustness – add state-specific linear trends ---------------------------
dt[, time_trend := period]             # create a running time variable
did_trend <- feols(y ~ treat_x_post + treated:time_trend | unit_id + period, 
                   data = dt, cluster = ~unit_id)

# 6. Print results -----------------------------------------------------------
cat("\n=== Main Two-Way FE DID ===\n")
print(summary(did_twfe))

cat("\nCoefficient of interest (treat_x_post): ", 
    round(coef(did_twfe)["treat_x_post"], 4), "\n")

cat("95% CI: ", round(confint(did_twfe, "treat_x_post"), 4), "\n")

cat("\n=== Plain DID (no FE) ===\n")
print(summary(did_plain))

cat("\n=== Placebo (pre-periods only) ===\n")
print(summary(placebo))

cat("\n=== DID with State Linear Trends ===\n")
print(summary(did_trend))
```



## 3. Expected Findings  
Theory and prior evidence (e.g., California’s 2004 PFL) suggest that paid family leave raises women’s attachment to the labor force by making career interruptions shorter and costlier to exit. We thus expect:

• Sign – Positive: β̂_treat×post > 0.  
• Magnitude – Modest but economically meaningful; a 0.02–0.05 log-point increase (≈ 2–5 %) in women’s labor-force participation.  

If the identifying assumptions hold, the main TWFE estimate should be significantly positive, the placebo estimate should be near zero and insignificant, and the result should survive the addition of state-specific trends.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: We compare changes in women's labor force participation in states with and without the law over time.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The implementation of paid family leave laws is associated with an increase in women's labor force participation.
